cells.tense: You're tending something and it's working because you're actually there while it happens.
cells.ask: Let one thing that's growing near you reach done without reaching for the next. Notice what's left in your hands.
cells.core:
You're tending something and it's growing on you — well, it is growing, and not because you're forcing it. You water it, you check the leaves, you let it get on with what it does. This is steady apprenticeship, keeping watch over something that isn't finished yet.

Becoming who you are shows up as this doing. Not a decision you'll make later, not some later claiming of yourself, but the ordinary hands-on care that anyone nearby can watch you give. Care that doesn't exhaust itself is rare, so notice when it isn't draining you. The moment something is done and you're still fussing over it, that's the only place to look. What you're doing is already you, and letting go of one finished thing is where the next of you shows up.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending it well — notice that.
cells.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them
cells.place: Standing where who you are is becoming visible

cells.tense: Before anything has a chance to be, you're already watering what might happen next week.
cells.ask: Stop one task before it needs you again. Do something with no use to the project at all, and let that stand for the day.
cells.core:
You see the finished shape before it's here and you're getting everything ready early, asking people if they've handled their part, fixing what isn't broken yet.

That push comes from real care, but it's a check on a season that hasn't started, and it misses the person sitting in front of you now. The thing you're dreaming of is a good one. It just hasn't finished cooking, and worry can't hurry something that grows at its own pace. Letting the future arrive on its own schedule isn't giving up on it. Your hands can be busy being useful. They don't have to be holding tomorrow too.

cells.tense: You're standing past a doorway where your own hands went quiet, and the quiet is still around you.
cells.ask: Pick the smallest living thing you've been upkeeping — the plant, the pot by the sink — and give it ten real minutes today.
cells.core:
The plant on the sill has been getting by. A neighbor's garden looks tended, and yours looks like it's waiting for you to come back to it. You can see what wants water. It just isn't reaching your hands yet.

Most of what you've been keeping going has been kept from a distance, and that distance has become normal. The move back is tiny. It isn't about fixing your whole grip on things, and it doesn't ask you to feel like a gardener first. One small living thing, given ten real minutes by you, gets your hands moving again. Picking up the watering can is enough to start.
cells.sheetLine: You pulled your hands back. The growing didn't leave.
cells.verb: Learning how things grow by tending them

cells.tense: You're already the one shaping this — you just call it the situation needing you.
cells.ask: Name one bit of upkeep you do and say plainly who keeps it going. Say it out loud to yourself once.
cells.core:
The little fixes, the reminders, the quiet arranging that keeps something alive: that's you being who you are, and you're describing it like it happened on its own. The upkeep runs fine, but the credit is going to nobody.

Becoming who you are needs you to see whose hands are doing it. Not as praise, not as a big word — just accurate. When you file your own steady care under 'it just needed doing', the next version of you has no address to arrive at. Claiming what you keep alive covers what's actually in your hands, not the whole story of who you've been. One true sentence about your own upkeep is enough to put the pen back in your hand.
cells.sheetLine: You're doing the upkeep. You just haven't claimed it.

attempts.check: The record supports apprenticeship (tending, learning how things grow) in this lived-in work; it doesn't say the person's parents, history, or early rooms are why it went quiet, so I only mark that a pause happened. An unsupported claim in my draft was 'you know you're deciding what to keep'; the record names the water — actualization, becoming the thing yourself — not what is in the person's mind, so I cut it. The other side of the card (care without exhaustion, holding without clutching) is where all four busy asks aim. If my read is wrong, the asks still make sense as ordinary tending. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about 'the work' instead of the thing actually in front of them, so the cells name hands, doorways, and moments instead.
